claims.text: Applying a thin chromium-based coating by physical vapor deposition to zirconium-alloy cladding improves resistance to high-temperature oxidation.
The chromium-based coating forms a continuous chromium oxide barrier during high-temperature oxidation.
The chromium oxide barrier limits oxygen diffusion into the cladding.
The initial zirconium-alloy cladding has the standard protective coating used under current service conditions.
CrN is an example of a chromium-based coating suitable for deposition on zirconium-alloy cladding by physical vapor deposition.
Temperatures around 800–1200°C are relevant to reactor transient events.
The coating will produce a continuous, adherent chromium oxide layer on the cladding surface.
The chromium-based coating oxidizes under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Oxidation of the coating produces a dense chromium oxide barrier.
Limiting oxygen diffusion reduces the oxidation kinetics of the zirconium alloy.
Coated cladding will have significantly lower oxidation rates than cladding having only the standard protective coating.
The lower oxidation rate will be observable as reduced weight gain.
The lower oxidation rate will be observable as a thinner oxide scale.
The beneficial effect depends on a uniform, defect-free coating with sufficient thickness to form a continuous chromium oxide layer.
A coating that is too thin or non-uniform may compromise mechanical integrity or thermal performance.
The magnitude of oxidation-rate reduction depends on coating thickness, coating uniformity, and oxidation severity.
